title: Forty thousand year old baby

paragraphs.text: On a May morning in 2007 a reindeer herder named Yuri Khudi stood with his sons on a sandbank in the Yuribey River in northwestern Siberia, looking at a diminutive corpse. Though they'd never seen such an animal before, they knew it well from stories their people, the Nenets, sang on dark winter nights. Khudi had seen many of the long honey-colored mammoth tusks that his people found each summer. But he had never seen an entire animal, let alone one so well preserved. Apart from its missing hair and toenails, it was perfectly intact.

Khudi was unsure what to do, so he traveled 150 miles south to consult with an old friend named Kirill Serotetto. Serotetto listened to his friend's story, then took him to see the director of the local museum, who persuaded the local authorities to fly Khudi and Serotetto back to the Yuribey River in a helicopter. When they arrived, the mammoth had vanished.

Khudi was aware that the now missing baby would be of enormous interest to the outside world. He also suspected that a person willing to handle such a thing would probably make a nice profit — ivory traders regularly visited the region to buy mammoth tusks, and who knows what they'd pay for an entire mammoth. Khudi's suspicions fell on one of his cousins, whom some locals had seen on the sandbank and later, riding away on his reindeer sled toward the town of Novyy Port.

When Khudi and Serotetto arrived at the town, they found the mammoth propped against the wall of a store. People were taking snapshots of it on their mobile phones. The shop owner had bought the body from Khudi's cousin for two snowmobiles and a year's worth of food. It wasn't until they had enlisted the help of local police that the friends finally managed to reclaim the mammoth. It was sent by helicopter to a museum in the regional capital, where grateful officials named the infant female Lyuba, after Khudi's wife. Since the first mammoth carcass was recovered in Siberia in 1806, about a dozen other soft-tissue specimens had been found, including several infants. Yet no carcass of any age was as intact as Lyuba.

One of the first scientists to see Lyuba was US palaeontologist Dan Fisher. Fisher could tell that she'd been in excellent condition at the time of her death. On the back of their neck, mammoths had a hump of fat, and in the case of Lyuba this was full and healthy — a further indication of her good physical state. Her condition appeared all the more mystifying in May 2008, when Fisher visited the Yuribey River. Just upriver from the sandbank where she'd been found stood a high, sheer bluff. Large blocks of permafrost hung over the rim of the bluff. Perhaps Lyuba had been frozen in such a block that had collapsed into the water during the previous thaw, floated downstream, and come to rest on the sandbank when the swollen river had briefly risen to that level.

There was only one problem: Khudi had found her there in May 2007, before the spring ice-out. The only explanation was that she had broken out of the permafrost and come to rest there nearly a year before being discovered, during the ice-out of June 2006. To Fisher, standing on the spot two years later, it just didn't make sense. She would have lain on the riverbank for an entire summer exposed to the sun. So why hadn't she decomposed or been scavenged by animals? The answers would have to come from Lyuba herself.

On June 4, 2008, an international team began a three-day series of tests and surgical procedures on Lyuba. As the flesh warmed, Fisher noticed an odd smell, which he found familiar but couldn't quite place. He observed that the mammoth's muscles were separated from the bone in places were, in a normal specimen, they would have been firmly bonded. Fisher also noted a dense mix of clay and sand in the mouth and throat, which would support the hypothesis that she'd died of suffocation, probably from breathing in river bank mud.

At the end of the autopsy, Fisher suddenly remembered where he had come across that smell before. It had come from some meat he had stored underwater during an experiment to find out how Palaeolithic hunters had kept mammoth meat from spoiling. Finally, Lyuba's superb state of preservation made sense. The microbes in the water had preserved her, like food preserved in vinegar. And the lactic acid they produced also could have caused the separation of muscles noticed during the autopsy. Finally, Lyuba's teeth revealed she had been born early in the spring and was a month old when she died. This conclusion was supported by the analysis of her tusk.

So Lyuba was probably killed by a misstep in or near a muddy river, and preserved for science by a combination of biochemical chance and the determination of a Nenets herder. Though studies are ongoing, she has already begun to shed the secrets of her short life and some clues to the fate of her species.
